prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength to reach fractional frequency uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean case of a new way of controlling atoms that changes what can be measured. Katori's magic-wavelength idea makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel while the atoms are held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil shifts, and this is a physical insight that nobody could have simply engineered around. Many atoms probed at once then give the statistics, and Jun Ye's group turned the concept into the accuracy frontier near 1e-18 and showed how to handle collisional and many-body effects. The result has been reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg by several laboratories, and clock comparisons over fibre links agree across continents, which is the kind of robustness and theory-experiment agreement I trust. It also says something concrete about nature: gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres, constancy of constants is tested to new levels, and the redefinition of the second is under way. The two-name credit is clean and needs no forced three-person compromise. I do not claim this is technologically motivated; as with the laser, the basic capability came first and the uses followed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier recognition. The 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, the comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control and clocks) cover the two pillars on which lattice clocks stand, so a committee could read this as an incremental advance within frequency metrology. The fundamental-physics payoffs so far are constraints, not discoveries: no drift of constants, no dark-matter signal. Priority is also not entirely tidy, since Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and others at PTB, SYRTE, NIST and JILA contributed in parallel. Against B018 specifically, I accept that topological insulators have the broadest support and a larger intellectual footprint in condensed matter, and that the clock case has to be made on the strength of the new capability rather than a new phase of matter.

responses.point: Kroll also ranks optical lattice clocks first and stresses the concrete, well-characterised systematics and timeliness, while worrying about distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock citations.
responses.response: We agree on the core of the case, but I do not want to accept that worry too quickly. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and the control of single ions; neither made a many-atom neutral-atom clock with Doppler- and recoil-free trapping, and the magic-wavelength condition is a genuinely new idea, not a refinement. I would still word the citation so that the lattice concept is explicit and the earlier prizes are not duplicated. Where I differ with him is on B027: he places atom interferometry second, and I rank it third. The priority history among Bordé, Pritchard, Chu and Kasevich is more tangled than for clocks, and Chu's 1997 prize makes me prefer clocks first.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a clean, verified, theory-to-experiment discovery that has reshaped condensed matter, mature for nearly two decades and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I take this seriously and ranked B018 fourth, not lower, because it is a new phase of matter distinguished by topology. My disagreement is about whether the trio is complete and clean. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that Molenkamp's HgTe experiment actually tested, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, lie partly outside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as several of us noted, so any prize here leaves a visible gap in the record. I defer to him and to the condensed-matter colleagues on how central the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is relative to the 3D materials. If the committee concludes that gap is acceptable, I would regard B018 as my first alternative, not a poor choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks kilonovae first and optical lattice clocks last in his ranking, regarding the clock as a measurement discovery with checkable outcomes but one whose fundamental-physics payoff so far is mainly null and which may seem incremental after earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: That is the fair version of the reservation, and I share part of it: a null result on the drift of constants is a constraint, not a discovery. But I would turn the argument around. A tool that has delivered a 1e-18 comparison of clocks showing gravitational redshift across a millimetre is already a discovery about how the laboratory can probe general relativity, and the null results are only as meaningful as the precision, which this method created. I would also note that B045 is built mostly on theory and on very large observational collaborations, and that the credit between the macronova proposers and the observers is, as he himself says, contested; the two-name clock credit has no comparable problem. I defer to him on how settled the r-process site question is.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and cold-atom quantum simulation second, arguing that both turned fundamental quantum theory into controllable laboratory systems, and flags that five credited names for B010 exceed the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree about B010: it was my second choice, and the five-name credit is the real difficulty. Jaksch is missing from the list, and Cirac and Dalibard are strong, so Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is defensible but leaves out major figures. This is why I would not make it my preferred prize even though I know the physics well. On circuit QED I am more cautious than he is. The strong-coupling experiment is excellent, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits sits very close in time and field, and the four-name credit forces a theory-experiment choice among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff. I would not put it ahead of clocks this year, and I note he has himself flagged a conflict on this topic.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first for being exact, universal and model-independent results that gave a new language for small driven systems, while noting that the credit is contested among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski, Crooks, Kurchan and others.
responses.response: I appreciate the appeal of exact results, and it is the sort of explanatory simplicity I like. I am out of my field here and defer to him on the experimental confirmations and on whether this is physics rather than chemistry territory. My difficulty is the attribution problem he states himself: with Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan and Crooks all arguably decisive, I cannot see a fair trio from the supplied credit. I would like him to say, for the committee, which contribution he regards as the one that a citation should name.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how a citation should word the lattice concept to make that clear.
Priority among Katori, Ye and the parallel Sr/Yb lattice-clock groups (PTB, SYRTE, NIST/JILA) is only partly known to me, and I cannot verify the dates from the materials available.
Whether the collaboration of topological-insulator credit can be made fair without Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Hasan; I defer to condensed-matter colleagues.
Whether a two-part prize is worth considering, since pairing B041 with a second achievement would exceed three people with any current B018 or B010 credit set.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041: my profile lists no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My known close ties are to Anne L'Huillier and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups (not on this shortlist) and to Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato; the general atomic, molecular and optical community overlap is a normal professional connection, not a recusal issue. I have no stated link to the candidates on B018, B010 or B027 either.
